info.description:
## Authentication

Operations require `Authorization: Bearer <api key>`; see the `ApiKeyBearer` security scheme. `/healthz`, `/readyz`, `/v1/status` and `/v1/auth/sso/exchange` take no API key.

## Errors

Failures use the envelope described by `#/components/responses/Error`: `{"success": false, "data": null, "error": {"code", "message", "details", "request_id"}}`. Common status codes: 400 (invalid input), 401 (missing or invalid key), 403 (key lacks the scope), 404 (not found), 409 (conflict with the current state), 413 (request body too large), 415 (a body that is not JSON), 416 (a download `Range` outside the file), 422 (request validation failed: `VALIDATION_ERROR` for a request that fails validation, `UNPROCESSABLE` for well-formed content the service refuses), 429 (rate limit or quota), 500 (internal error), 503 (node unavailable or no capacity; see `Retry-After`).

Every 409 `CONFLICT` carries `error.details.reason`, a stable string to switch on instead of parsing the message. The values:
- `name_taken`: a sandbox, volume or snapshot with that name already exists in the org
- `already_exists`: the object (member, external id, file, row id) already exists
- `concurrent_update`: another writer changed the row first; retry
- `no_container`: the sandbox has no running container for the call
- `in_progress`: the same work (idempotency key, snapshot) has not finished yet
- `in_use`: the object is still used by a sandbox
- `closed`: the PTY or session is closed or does not accept the call
- `operation_failed`: a git or fs command in the sandbox failed
- `changed_during_reset`: the sandbox changed state while a reset replaced it
- `unsupported_mode`: the operation is not supported in the configured run mode
- `disk_full`: the runtime reported that the sandbox disk is full
- `runtime_conflict`: the runtime refused the operation for another reason
- `result_unavailable`: a keyed exec already ran, but its answer was not kept for replay (error code `IDEMPOTENCY_RESULT_UNAVAILABLE`); the command does not run again
- `conflict`: fallback when none of the above applies

A 409 `INVALID_STATE` (an operation the current state does not allow) carries `error.details.state`.

The `Idempotency-Key` header (1 to 255 characters; an empty or longer key answers 422 `VALIDATION_ERROR`) is accepted by exactly these operations: create sandbox (`POST /v1/sandboxes`), synchronous exec (`POST /v1/sandboxes/{sandbox_id}/toolbox/process/execute`), code run (`POST /v1/sandboxes/{sandbox_id}/toolbox/process/code-run`), create session (`POST /v1/sandboxes/{sandbox_id}/toolbox/process/sessions`), register snapshot (`POST /v1/snapshots`), snapshot from sandbox (`POST /v1/snapshots/from-sandbox`), create volume (`POST /v1/volumes`). Every other POST ignores the header. Reusing a key with a different request body answers 422 `IDEMPOTENCY_MISMATCH`; a request whose key is still in progress answers 409 with reason `in_progress`. A replay of a stored answer carries the `Idempotent-Replayed: true` response header.

A query parameter an operation does not declare is refused with 422 `VALIDATION_ERROR`, one `details.errors` entry of type `extra_forbidden` per unknown name (`loc` is `["query", <name>]`). A method a path does not support answers 405 `METHOD_NOT_ALLOWED` with an `Allow` header.

Every response carries the `x-request-id` header (a well-formed client-supplied value is kept), and error bodies repeat it as `error.request_id`; quote it when reporting a failure.

The exec and code-run results (`/toolbox/process/execute` and `/toolbox/process/code-run`) carry `stop_reason`, null for a normal exit. The values:
- `timeout`: the command reached `timeout_s`
- `output_limit`: the output limit was reached and the output is truncated
- `sandbox_stopped`: the sandbox stopped under the command: it was stopped (by a caller or by auto-stop), or it died (a resource limit was hit or its main process ended); stderr says which
- `sandbox_deleted`: the sandbox was deleted while the command ran
- `sandbox_reset`: the sandbox was reset while the command ran
- `oom_killed`: the sandbox ran out of memory and the server could see it: the container died of it (`sandbox_stopped` is true) or the kernel killed the process (the sandbox keeps running); the container isolation tier only, the gVisor and microVM tiers still answer `killed` or `sandbox_stopped`

get.description:
Export the org's audit events as NDJSON, one chained row per line.

Each line carries the event plus its ``prev_hash`` and ``hash``, in chain order.
The optional ``from`` (inclusive) and ``to`` (exclusive) bound ``occurred_at``; the
optional ``request_id`` and ``outcome`` keep only rows that match exactly, as in the list
route. Any other query parameter is rejected with 422 naming it.

The last line is always a trailer, told apart from rows by its `type` field:

- `audit_head` (the line the operator `audit-export` writes: `org_id`, `row_id`, `hash`,
  `hmac`) when the server has an audit chain key and the export holds at least one row. It
  names the LAST ROW OF THIS EXPORT (`row_id`, `hash`), which is the org's newest chain row
  unless a `to` bound cut the export earlier. `hmac` is HMAC-SHA256 with the chain key over
  the row id and its hash (and the content fields below), so a holder of the key can detect
  a truncated export and anchor `audit-verify --head` on it. The head also binds the
  content of this export: `row_count` (the number of event lines above it), `first_row_id`
  (the id of the first one) and `export_sha256` (hex SHA-256 over the exact UTF-8 bytes of
  every event line, each with its trailing newline, in order; not the trailer). They are
  covered by the HMAC and by the signature, so an auditor can recompute them from the file
  and detect any added, removed, reordered or edited line. With a `request_id` or `outcome`
  filter the export is not a contiguous run of the chain, so the head carries `filtered:
  true` and `filters` (the filter values given, as text): a reader checks the content
  binding but not the neighbour linkage of the rows.
  When the server also has an audit signing key (an Ed25519 key), the head carries `alg`
  (`ed25519`), `public_key` and `signature` (urlsafe base64) and `signed_at` (when the
  server signed it, UTC ISO 8601 to the second, e.g. `2026-11-11T04:52:33+00:00`): a
  signature over the canonical JSON (keys sorted, compact) of the head without `signature`
  and `hmac`, so `signed_at` and the content fields are covered. An auditor checks it with
  the public key alone (`audit_public_key` of `GET /v1/status`, the same key that signs),
  which proves the export has the content the server signed at `signed_at`; of two signed
  heads, the later `signed_at` is the newer one. The keyed row hashes themselves can only be
  recomputed with the chain key.
- `export_summary` (`rows`, the number of rows in this export, and `filters`, the sorted
  names of the filters given) otherwise: an empty export, or a server without a chain key.
  It names no row and is not signed.

Rows and trailer are read in one unit of work, so the head never names a row the export
did not include.

A label-scoped API key gets 403 Forbidden: audit events are org-wide, not scoped to
sandboxes.

get.description:
Verify the caller org's audit hash chain.

Takes only ``from_id``; any other query parameter is rejected with 422 naming it.

Walks the whole chain, page by page, as ``audit-verify`` does for one org, and
reports the rows checked, the first and last ids and any findings.

With ``from_id`` the walk starts at that row: its own hash is still recomputed and
checked, but its link to the row before it is taken as the trust anchor, and every
later row is checked as in a full walk. Such a verify proves the chain from that row
on, not the history before it; the response names the row in ``anchor_id``. An id
that is unknown or belongs to another org answers 404.

A label-scoped API key gets 403 Forbidden: audit events are org-wide, not scoped to
sandboxes.

Re-anchor: an operator can run `audit-reanchor` to acknowledge historical breaks. It
appends an `audit.chain_reanchored` event naming the last row with a finding
(`acknowledged_through`). Findings on rows at or before that row are counted in
`acknowledged_findings`, named by `reanchored_by`, and no longer make `ok` false.
`reanchor` carries that event's operator, reason code, note, finding count and time
(left out when there is none), so the verify alone tells who acknowledged what and why.
It acknowledges, it never hides: no row is changed or removed, the full history stays
in the export, and a break after that row, in the re-anchor event itself or after it
still makes `ok` false. `findings` lists only unacknowledged findings.

post.description:
Start a persistent Python kernel inside the started sandbox, like a notebook kernel. Variables, imports and loaded data survive from one run to the next. `cwd` sets the kernel's working directory and defaults to the sandbox's working directory; the response returns the resolved `cwd`. Only `python` is supported, and the sandbox image must have `python3`, otherwise the create is refused with 409. The context lives in the kernel process, so it is lost when the sandbox is reset, stopped (auto-stop included) or deleted; files written to disk are not affected. Needs the `toolbox:use` scope.

`name` is optional. Uniqueness among the live contexts of the sandbox is enforced per API process: two creates of one name that race across processes may both succeed. A create with the name of a live context returns that context with 200 instead of starting a new one (201); its `cwd` is kept and the `cwd` of the request is ignored, so the reply carries the existing context's `cwd`. A name no live context has starts a new one. If the live contexts cannot be read (a driver failure), the create fails instead of starting a context. After a stop and start the same call brings a context of that name back, with empty state.

200.description: A live context already has the requested `name`: that existing context is returned instead of a new one. Its `cwd` is kept and the `cwd` of the request is ignored.

delete.description: Kill the kernel of the context and remove its directory at once, without the 2 s grace a run gives a stuck cell; its state is gone. Answers 404 for an unknown id. A cell that is running on the context when it is deleted ends with `stop_reason` `context_lost`. Besides this call, a context is removed only by a run whose exec deadline passed with the cell still not answering after the 2 s grace (see the run operation); the timeout of a cell and an interrupt request keep it.

post.description:
Send an interrupt (SIGINT) to the kernel of the context. A running cell raises `KeyboardInterrupt` in Python code, which is a cell error, and the state stays; between cells there is nothing to interrupt and the answer is `interrupted: false`. The route names no cell, so it interrupts whichever cell is running at that moment.

This is the same sequence the run operation describes. A cell's own `timeout_s` ends it with `TimeoutError` once control is back in Python, and this call does the same at once when it can. It cannot stop a cell stuck in native code (a long C call or a ctypes sleep that never returns to Python): that cell goes on, and later runs on the context queue behind it, each for up to its own `queue_timeout`, until the cell ends at its `timeout_s` or the run's exec deadline passes. This call never stops the kernel or removes the context; that happens only to a run whose exec deadline passed with the cell still not answering, and the kernel is stopped and the context removed only after that 2 s grace; later runs then answer 404. `interrupted` is `true` when a cell was running and the kernel was sent the interrupt, and `false` when no cell is running or the context has no live kernel. Each call is audited as `toolbox.code_contexts.interrupt`.
post.summary: Interrupt the running cell of a code context

post.description:
Run a cell of Python code in the context; state from earlier cells is still there. The response has every field of `/process/code-run` (`stdout`, `stderr`, `exit_code`, `timed_out`, `stop_reason`) plus `result`, the `repr` of the cell's trailing expression (`null` when there is none or the cell raised), and `error`, `{type, message}` of the exception the cell raised (`null` otherwise). `result` and the error text are cut to 4096 characters. A cell that raises exits 1.

Cells of one context are serialized: runs on one context queue and run in order. A run that waits longer than its own `timeout_s` answers exit code 124, `timed_out` and `stop_reason` `queue_timeout`; it never started and the context is kept, so send the cell again.

How a cell that does not finish ends, in order:

1. `timeout_s` limits one cell. It fires inside the kernel when control is back in Python and ends the cell with `TimeoutError`; the result reports `timed_out` and the state stays.
2. `POST .../interrupt` does the same at once when it can. A cell stuck in native code (a long C call or a ctypes sleep that never returns to Python) does not stop, and later runs on the context queue behind it, each for up to its own `queue_timeout`, until the cell ends at 1 or 3. Interrupt requests never remove the context.
3. Only when this run's exec deadline (`timeout_s` plus a 5 s margin) passes with the cell still not answering is the kernel sent an interrupt and given 2 s. A kernel that answers keeps its context, and the run ends with `stop_reason` `timeout`. One that does not is stopped and the context removed only after that 2 s grace, so later runs on it answer 404; that run ends with `stop_reason` `context_lost`, `exit_code` 124 and `timed_out` true, and its stderr says the context was stopped. A cell that ends at 1 (the kernel answered, state kept) is a plain `timeout`.

A run can end at 1 or 3 and can queue as in 2; an interrupt request can only cause 2; `DELETE` removes the context at once.

`stdout` is capped at 1 MiB minus 64 KiB, which leaves room for `result` and `error`. A run that hits the cap ends with `stop_reason` `output_limit`; its cell is interrupted and the context and its state are kept. When the client of a run disconnects or the run is cancelled, the run's own cell is interrupted (never a later run's cell) before the next run can start.

Other stop reasons: `context_lost` when the kernel died or closed the connection during the run, the context was deleted mid-run, or the kernel was stopped and the context removed after the exec deadline and the 2 s grace (see 3). The contexts are lost when the sandbox is reset, stopped (auto-stop included) or deleted. Scope, label scope, audit rows and error mapping are those of `/process/code-run`.
post.summary: Run a cell in a code context

post.description:
Run a cell of Python code in the context and receive its output as server-sent events while it runs. The request body is that of the run operation, and so are the rules: runs on one context are serialized and wait up to `timeout_s` (`queue_timeout`), `timeout_s` and the exec deadline end a cell as described there, `stdout` is capped at 1 MiB minus 64 KiB (`output_limit`), and a client that disconnects interrupts its own cell.

The stream has `stdout` and `stderr` events, `data: {"data": <text>}`, one per chunk the driver delivers (UTF-8, invalid bytes replaced), then exactly one final `result` event whose data is the object the run operation answers in `data` (`stdout`, `stderr`, `exit_code`, `timed_out`, `truncated`, `stop_reason`, `result`, `error`, ...). `stdout` is forwarded by whole lines: the last line, without its newline yet, is held back until its newline or the end of the run, and the outcome line the platform's client prints last is never sent (the `result` event carries it as `result` and `error`). `stderr` is forwarded as it arrives. The `result` event holds the complete `stdout` and `stderr`, including lines the platform adds to `stderr` after the exec ended.

An unknown context, a sandbox that is not started and the scope and label checks answer as for run, with the error envelope, before the stream starts. A failure after the stream started sends one `error` event, `data: {"code": <error code>, "message": <text>}`, instead of `result`, and ends the stream. Scope, label scope and the audit rows (action `toolbox.code_contexts.run_stream`, the details of run) are those of run.

200.description: Server-sent events (no envelope). One `stdout` or `stderr` event per output chunk of the cell, `data: {"data": <text>}`; `stdout` is sent by whole lines, so the last line arrives with its newline or at the end, and the outcome line of the client is never sent. One final `result` event, whose data is the object the run operation answers in `data`, ends the stream. A failure after the stream started sends one `error` event, `data: {"code": <error code>, "message": <text>}`, instead of `result`. The events carry no `id`, so a dropped stream cannot be resumed: a new request is a new run. While idle the server sends a `: keepalive` comment line about every 15 seconds; each `data:` line is one JSON object.

If-Range is compared to the weak ETag; this deviates from RFC 9110, which forbids weak validators there, so a changed file with an unchanged mtime could resume wrongly.

post.description:
Run a command in the sandbox and wait for its result.

With an `Idempotency-Key` header the same key and body replays the first response and the
command does not run again; the key is kept for one day (24 hours) after the response is
stored. The same key with another body answers 422; a body is compared as the API reads it,
so spelling a default out (`timeout_s` 60 or 60.0, `"env": {}`, `"stdin": null`) is the same
body. The key belongs to the API key and the sandbox, and a failed attempt does not keep it.
Replays carry `Idempotent-Replayed: true` and are audited as `sandbox.exec.replay`.

A replay needs the sandbox started, as a first run does; after a reset of the sandbox, or a
stop and a new start, the command runs again. A result cut short by a stop, delete or reset
of the sandbox (`stop_reason` `sandbox_stopped`, `sandbox_deleted` or `sandbox_reset`, as
the service reads it from the sandbox) is not kept, so a retry runs the command. A
`sandbox_stopped` that only reports a death under a limit, while the sandbox still reads
started, is kept like any other answer. When stdout plus stderr exceed
256 KiB or the output was truncated, the output is not kept: a retry answers 409
`IDEMPOTENCY_RESULT_UNAVAILABLE` and the command does not run again; that replay is audited
`denied` with reason `result_unavailable`.

The command runs at most once per server process while it runs; after a crash between the
command finishing and the answer being stored, a retry may run it again.

Download the contents of a volume as a gzipped tar (`application/gzip`), streamed with a `Content-Disposition: attachment` file name taken from the volume name (`<name>.tar.gz`). The Docker daemon reads the volume through a helper container that is created but never started (no process runs, no network), with the volume mounted read-only; the tar it returns is gzipped as it streams. A volume that a running sandbox mounts can be exported too: it is read while the sandbox may still write, so files can change during the read and the archive is not a point in time snapshot. Stop the sandboxes first when you need a consistent copy. A read that fails after the first bytes were sent ends the body early, so the download is incomplete. The key must own the volume through its labels: a volume reached only through `shared_volume_labels` answers 403, an unseen one 404. A driver without volume transfer answers 409 `CONFLICT` with reason `unsupported_mode`, and a volume being restored 409 with reason `restore_in_progress`. At most `SANDFORT_MAX_VOLUME_TRANSFERS_PER_ORG` (2) exports and restores per organization and `SANDFORT_MAX_VOLUME_TRANSFERS` (8) per server process run at once; over it answers 409 with reason `org_transfer_limit` or `transfer_limit` (restore shares these caps). The export is audited as `volume.export` before the first byte; the row names the volume, and the byte count is not known at that point.

post.description: Replace the contents of a volume with a gzipped tar sent as the raw request body. The volume is emptied first (removed and created again, same name and labels) and then the Docker daemon extracts the archive through a helper container that is created but never started (no process runs, no network), so a restore is not atomic: a restore that fails after it began leaves the volume EMPTY, and the error says so (`error.details.volume_emptied`). Refused with 409 `CONFLICT` (reason `in_use`) while any sandbox that is not deleted mounts the volume, and with reason `restore_in_progress` while another restore of the volume runs. The body may be up to 256 MiB compressed: a `Content-Length` above that answers 413 before the body is read. The restored data is counted as it is extracted and must stay within the volume size limit (`SANDFORT_VOLUME_MAX_BYTES`, when one is set); over it answers 413 and leaves the volume empty. A body that is not gzip or is empty answers 422 and changes nothing; a gzip body that is corrupt, cut short or not a tar answers 422 and leaves the volume empty. Without a size limit the decompressed size is still capped at 64 times the compressed size (never below 16 MiB; the declared `Content-Length`, or the bytes received so far when the body is chunked): over it answers 413 with `details.max_expansion_ratio` and leaves the volume empty. Only regular files, directories and symlinks with a relative target inside the volume are accepted; modes (setuid and sticky bits included), uid, gid and modification times are restored as the tar records them, extended attributes are not. Any other member answers 422 with `error.details.reason` `forbidden_entry`, `details.violation` naming the rule (`path_traversal`, `absolute_path`, `invalid_name`, `invalid_link_target`, `hardlink`, `symlink_absolute`, `symlink_escape`, `symlink_through`, `duplicate_entry` (a second member whose normalised path equals an earlier member's, whatever the types), `special_file`, `unsupported_entry`, `header_too_large`, `too_many_entries`) and `details.entry` the member, and leaves the volume empty. The key must own the volume through its labels (403 for a volume reached only through `shared_volume_labels`, 404 for an unseen one). The result is audited as `volume.restore` with the restored bytes, or with the failure and whether the volume was emptied.

413.description: Error code `PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE`. Three causes: a `Content-Length` over 256 MiB (refused before the body is read, nothing changes; `error.details` is `{limit_bytes, size_bytes}`); more bytes sent than that without a declared length; or the extracted data over the volume size limit (`details.limit_bytes`) or over 64 times the compressed size (`details.max_expansion_ratio`), which leaves the volume empty (`details.volume_emptied` is `true`).

A cursor is bound to this endpoint and to the ``event_type`` and ``state`` filters; one
presented with another endpoint or other filters answers 422 naming the differing field.
Rows written before the delivery detail migration carry no ``event_type`` and so never
match that filter. The dispatcher fills it in when it loads such a delivery (a pending one
that is due, whether it is then sent or parked); a pre-migration row that is already
delivered, failed or parked stays without one until a redelivery makes it due again.
The server scans at most ``10 x`` the max page size (``SCAN_CAP`` = 1000) rows per request;
when a filter skips so many rows that the bound is reached first, the page may be short
or empty and ``meta.next_cursor`` points at the last scanned row, so the client continues
from the cursor until it is ``null``.

post.description:
Requeue a dead (``failed``) or parked (``disabled``) delivery; a delivered one is final.

A new cycle starts: attempts go back to 0 and the delivery is ``pending`` and due at once.
``next_attempt_at`` stays null: the API process clock never schedules a send (a worker
whose clock is behind would delay it); the dispatcher stamps the time on its next attempt.
The attempt history is kept and a ``redelivered`` entry naming the calling key is
appended; the last status and the last error are cleared together.
